title: Growing the band and a trip to record at Edison
summary: With more saxophones in the band, he describes a Lafayette College group making an acoustic Edison record.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Making records: studios, takes and the technology

blocks.x: In the third year, I got another saxophone player. That's three saxophone players, trumpet and trombone and we got along nicely with that. Everything was beginning to sound a little bit better, fuller. Now all this time in the development of orchestras, particularly local orchestras and even back like the Whiteman, where they had two saxophones, that was like maybe my freshman year or something. The tendency was to expand the harmonies and even the recording companies liked that because they were delving into electronics in those days, They would give you the orthophonic and they would give -- I played with an orchestra my freshman year, I went down to Lafayette College to play with a friend of mine and they had a date to make a record at Edison.

So we went down there and if we didn't go into a little room and each one was on a different ladder and each one had a different horn to blow in, and I remember that experience. I never had that after and I -- but that was the experience of the records and when you bought that thick Edison record and they started everything off and "this is by so and so like it was coming out of a distant place, and this would start, the title would give and it's sung by the Edison record -- or made by or something like that," sung by so and so of the Edison

records," and that you could -- it was very pipey, but after that with the Whiteman, you're beginning to get other records that were pretty good, but they all sounded Mickey Mousish, you know, they were up in the upper stratus, there were no heavy basses in there.
